title: How Women Over 40 Can Stop Being Invisible | Ep 69
guestBio: Mel Elsbeth is a Harvard-certified visibility and brand strategist who spent years building award-winning marketing campaigns for global powerhouses like Diageo and Red Bull — all while hiding her own name behind their logos. After navigating 35+ roles across 15+ industries, she now helps women over 40 articulate their value, own their story, and attract aligned opportunities through her Brand Story Sessions. She is also the host of the Mama What's Next podcast, a show celebrating working moms and founders who turn the motherhood advantage into sustainable, fulfilling businesses.
excerpt: If you've spent years being the most capable person in the room while somehow remaining the least visible, this episode is for you. Visibility strategist Mel Elsbeth joins Aimee to reveal why accomplished women hide — and the one authentic tool that can change everything. Your expertise is not the problem. Being unseen is.
metaDescription: Visibility strategist Mel Elsbeth shows women over 40 how to build a personal brand, get seen professionally, and stop hiding behind their résumé.
keyTakeaways: Staying quietly in the background doesn't keep you safe — it actively blocks your career growth and professional development.
Playing it safe makes your message forgettable; real connection and credibility come from honest, human storytelling that shows who you actually are.
In the AI economy, everyone searches for you online before they trust you, which means credibility now requires proof that lives beyond your résumé.
You don't need a podcast, a newsletter, AND a YouTube channel — you need exactly one visibility tool that genuinely fits your voice and that you'll actually use consistently.
A single visibility asset gives you a measurable edge: employers and clients invest more time and money in people they can already see, hear, and trust.
The coordination, nurturing, emotional intelligence, and logistical mastery women develop through motherhood are not soft skills — they are undervalued leadership capabilities.
Visibility isn't about becoming louder or more performative; it's about becoming more honest and letting the right people finally find you.

quiz.title: What's Your Visibility Blind Spot?
quiz.description: You've built the skills. You've done the work. But something keeps you from stepping fully into the spotlight — and it's different for every woman. Take this self-discovery quiz to uncover your unique visibility pattern and find out exactly what your next move looks like.

A.name: The Quiet Powerhouse
A.description: You are undeniably capable, and the people close to you know it — but you've built a professional life that keeps your name comfortably out of the headline. You're drawn to systems, results, and doing the work rather than talking about it, and there's real integrity in that. The challenge is that your impact stays local when it could be global, and the opportunities that would light you up are going to the people who showed up online while you were busy delivering. This episode will feel like someone finally said out loud what you've been quietly feeling for years.

B.name: The Reluctant Storyteller
B.description: You know you have something worth saying — you can feel it — but every time you go to put it out there, the internal editor shows up and talks you out of it. What if it's not good enough? What if someone disagrees? What if you sound arrogant? You soften the message until it says nothing, and then wonder why it didn't land. Mel's conversation about playing it safe will hit differently for you, because you already know the problem. This episode gives you the framework — and the permission — to finally say the real thing.

C.name: The Momentum Seeker
C.description: You've dabbled. You started the Instagram, drafted the newsletter, recorded a few videos — and then life happened, consistency slipped, and the whole thing quietly faded. It's not that you lack ideas or enthusiasm; you have plenty of both. What you haven't found yet is the one format that fits so naturally that it doesn't feel like one more thing to manage. Mel's 'one tool' philosophy was made for you, and this episode will help you stop scattered starting and find the single visibility asset that will actually compound over time.

D.name: The Identity Rebuilder
D.description: You're in a season of change — whether that's re-entering the workforce, pivoting industries, stepping out of a role that no longer fits, or finally building something of your own. You know you need to put yourself out there, but you're not entirely sure who 'yourself' is right now in professional terms. That uncertainty is not a weakness; it's actually the most honest place to start building a brand from. Mel's story of stepping out from behind the big brand logos and into her own voice will feel like a road map specifically written for this chapter of your life.

content:
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from being excellent at your work and invisible at the same time. You deliver. You lead. You solve the problems nobody else wants to touch. And somehow, when it's time for the promotion, the contract, the speaking invitation, or the next big opportunity — someone else's name comes up first. Someone louder. Someone who showed up online. Someone who, frankly, may not be doing the work as well as you.

That gap between capability and visibility is exactly what this episode tears open. Aimee sits down with Mel Elsbeth — Harvard-certified brand strategist, host of the Mama What's Next podcast, and a woman who spent years making billion-dollar brands famous while keeping herself completely anonymous — for one of the most honest conversations this show has ever had about why accomplished women stay hidden, and what it actually costs them.

The Woman Behind the Brand

Mel's backstory is not what you'd expect from someone who now teaches visibility for a living. She grew up in East Germany as the quiet one — the observer — in a bold, brave family that marched front row in the 1989 peaceful revolution. That context matters, because it tells you something important: staying in the background was a deeply formed identity for Mel, not a preference. She carried it into a distinguished corporate marketing career, working behind global juggernauts like Diageo and Red Bull, building brand equity for companies while skillfully avoiding the spotlight herself.

"I was hiding in my jobs," she says without flinching. "Big brands are a beautiful place to disappear — until disappearing starts costing you." That line alone should stop you mid-scroll. Because if you've ever found comfort in being the person behind the scenes, the one who lets the work speak for itself, the one who figures the right people will notice eventually — Mel is talking directly to you.

What Visibility Actually Costs You When You Avoid It

This episode doesn't traffic in vague motivational language. Mel is refreshingly specific about the professional mechanics of invisibility. When you step back — even gracefully, even strategically — in corporate environments, there are real consequences. Promotions go to people who are seen thinking out loud, not just delivering quietly. Clients choose the person they've already heard from, not the one with the better track record buried in a PDF. And in the AI economy, where anyone can be searched, summarized, and vetted in thirty seconds, the absence of a digital presence reads as a red flag, not humility.

Your résumé got you here. It will not get you to what's next. That is Mel's core argument, and it is difficult to argue with. She walks through the practical reality: hiring managers, potential collaborators, and clients are checking for you online before they ever pick up the phone. What they find — or don't find — shapes the conversation before it begins. If nothing comes up, you are asking them to take a risk that your visible competitors are not asking them to take.

The One Tool You Actually Need

Here is where Mel's advice diverges from the overwhelming noise of the content marketing industrial complex. She is not telling you to be everywhere. She is not building you a twelve-platform strategy or a content calendar that requires a team to execute. She is telling you to pick one visibility tool — one format, one platform, one consistent place where people can encounter the real you — and do that with full commitment.

For some women, that's a podcast. For others, it's a newsletter, a LinkedIn presence, or even a well-crafted application video that shows personality instead of just credentials. The format is almost irrelevant. What matters is that it's authentic to how you actually communicate, and that you will realistically maintain it. Mel's own podcast, Mama What's Next, has generated work opportunities that didn't exist five years ago — speaking engagements, brand partnerships, client relationships — simply because people could hear her thinking, trust her voice, and decide she was the right person before she ever pitched herself.

That is the power of a visibility asset. It works while you sleep, while you're running carpool, while you're managing a team. It is the professional foundation that compounds over time in ways that hustle alone simply cannot.

Playing It Safe Is the Riskiest Move You Can Make

One of the most uncomfortable truths Mel surfaces in this conversation is about the quality of what most women put out when they do show up publicly. Trying not to offend anyone. Trying to appeal to everyone. Keeping it professional, polished, and perfectly palatable. The result? Content that says nothing, connects with nobody, and disappears instantly.

Playing it safe doesn't protect you. It just makes your message so bland that nobody remembers you were even in the room. Real connection — the kind that builds trust, generates referrals, and creates long-term professional relationships — comes from honesty. From sharing the actual struggle, the real opinion, the specific experience. From sounding like a human being instead of a LinkedIn template.

This is a lesson Aimee knows intimately. The Manage Her® was built on the belief that women in leadership deserve conversations that are real, not curated — and Mel's framework is a direct extension of that philosophy into how you show up for your own career and business.

The Invisible Load Is Leadership Experience in Disguise

The conversation takes a powerful turn when it reaches the territory of motherhood. Mel is direct: the skills women develop while raising children, managing households, and coordinating complex family logistics are not separate from professional leadership — they are professional leadership. The emotional intelligence, the crisis management, the ability to hold multiple competing priorities without dropping any of them, the capacity to nurture growth in people who are actively trying your patience — these are exactly the skills that make extraordinary leaders.

The problem is that women have been conditioned to keep these two worlds separate. To apologize for the school pickup call. To hide the invisible load instead of naming it as evidence of their range. Mel argues — and Aimee agrees — that the future of female leadership looks like integration, not compartmentalization. It looks like operating at 80% capacity with full results, because you've built systems, set boundaries, and stopped performing the myth of seamless availability.

The Permission You've Been Waiting For

By the end of this episode, something shifts. The conversation between Aimee and Mel is not a lecture. It's a mirror. And what it reflects back is this: the discomfort you feel about being seen is not a signal to stay hidden. It's a signal that something important is ready to move.

You have spent years building expertise, relationships, and results. You have been carrying leadership skills in every room you've walked into — professional and personal. The only thing standing between where you are and where you want to go is letting people see what you're actually made of. Not louder. Not more polished. Just more honest.

This episode will lovingly, firmly, and very specifically call your bluff. Press play.
